Full text

Abstract

Debates across the behavioral sciences have long examined whether ambiguity avoidance in decision making reflects stable preferences for certainty or uncertainty in beliefs formed through limited experience. Prior studies have commonly used the max-min expected utility (MMEU) model to interpret ambiguity-related decisions, but MMEU confounds preferences with beliefs by focusing on the range of possible probabilities rather than how individuals form them. We conducted two experiments (N = 53; N = 298) using a Linked Colored Lottery Task to test whether ambiguity avoidance reflects stable preferences or beliefs about outcome distributions. Participants first learned to associate colors with distinct outcome distributions by sampling from them and then made incentivized choices between options that varied in ambiguity. This design allowed us to observe how beliefs about distributional variance influenced decisions and to distinguish whether choices reflected belief construction versus uncertainty evaluation. We compared models based on MMEU and on subjective recursive expected utility (SREU), which explicitly separates beliefs from preferences. In both experiments, model comparison favored SREU, and participants with more dispersed inferred beliefs were more likely to avoid ambiguous options. Sampling patterns and memory for probabilities showed similar effects.

Apparent age-related differences in ambiguity avoidance were also better explained by belief variance than by preferences. These results suggest that ambiguity avoidance often reflects perceived imprecision in learned beliefs rather than an inherent aversion to uncertainty, plausibly a cognitive rather than affective phenomenon, with implications for understanding decision making across learning, memory, and uncertainty processing domains.

1 Introduction

Most consequential decisions involve ambiguity, situations where the probabilities of outcomes are unknown rather than explicitly stated. From retirement planning and medical treatment choices to career decisions and financial investments, people routinely make choices without knowing the precise likelihood of success (Dimmock et al., 2016; Portnoy et al., 2013; Xu & Adams, 2020). Rather than treating such uncertainty as risk and forming internal probability estimates, people consistently undervalue ambiguous options, a phenomenon known as ambiguity aversion (Ellsberg, 1961; Tanaka et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2020).

While ambiguity aversion has been documented across diverse contexts, researchers have long debated what drives it. Some theories attribute it to pessimism (Pulford, 2009) or discomfort (Golman, Gurney, & Loewenstein, 2021) with unknown probabilities. However, ambiguity aversion may also emerge from the way individuals internally represent and evaluate uncertain probability distributions, motivating computational models that distinguish beliefs about outcomes from preferences over uncertainty itself (Halevy, 2007). To formalize these ideas, several computational models have been proposed to capture how people evaluate uncertain options. These models differ in whether they treat beliefs and preferences as separate psychological constructs, and they make diverging predictions about behavior in ambiguous situations.

The rising popularity of computational modeling in psychology and neuroscience has provided powerful new tools for quantifying individual differences in cognition, emotion, and decision making (Patzelt, Hartley, & Gershman, 2018). Many of these models are derived from economics and have been applied to explain how people evaluate risky choices, delayed rewards, and ambiguous outcomes. In clinical and developmental research, such approaches have helped link patterns of decision making to age, stress, and substance use, among other factors (e.g., Tymula et al., 2012; FeldmanHall et al., 2016; Konova et al., 2020). However, the interpretation of these findings depends critically on the modeling framework used, as different models can attribute behavior to distinct underlying mechanisms.

One prominent framework is the max-min expected utility (MMEU) model (Gilboa & Schmeidler, 1989), which assumes that individuals react solely to the range of possible outcomes, treating all probability distributions within that range as equivalent. Consider a lottery with winning probabilities between 30% and 70%. MMEU predicts identical behavior whether people believe the true probability clusters around 50% or skews toward the extremes, yet these different beliefs may produce different choices. This limitation has motivated alternative models. The recursive expected utility (REU) framework (Klibanoff & Ozdenoren, 2007; Halevy, 2007; Klibanoff et al., 2009) explicitly separates preferences from beliefs, recognizing that people may construct subjective probability distributions over unknown outcomes and that decision making depends on both the properties of those distributions (e.g., mean, variance, shape) and individuals' attitudes toward uncertainty. This framework allows researchers to ask whether behavioral differences reflect how people form beliefs about uncertainty or how they evaluate those outcomes once beliefs are in place. Clarifying this distinction is important not only for economic modeling but also for psychological theories of learning, memory, and choice. By highlighting how ambiguity-avoidant behavior may arise from differences in belief construction rather than stable preferences, this work contributes to a more nuanced understanding of decision making under uncertainty.

Evidence supporting this distinction between beliefs and preferences comes from studies where participants make choices over explicitly described probability distributions. When participants choose between lotteries with identical expected values but different variance of probabilities, they show systematic preferences for lower-variance options (Halevy, 2007; Bach et al., 2011; Chapman et al., 2023). Such findings directly contradict MMEU's predictions but align with REU's framework, suggesting that variance sensitivity, not just range sensitivity, drives behavior under ambiguity. However, most existing paradigms rely on artificial scenarios where the variance in probabilities is explicitly described, which breaks conditions of ambiguity (i.e., conditions where the probabilities are unknown) and fails to capture how people may naturally learn about ambiguous situations. In the real world, ambiguity is rarely presented as explicit probability ranges. Instead, people must infer uncertainty from experience, forming beliefs about likely outcomes based on past observations, expert opinions, and contextual cues. Recent work shows people often ignore absent causes and favor simpler explanations, implying that cognitive representations can omit negations, a mechanism that could systematically bias how beliefs are formed under uncertainty (Vrantsidis & Lombrozo, 2025). These beliefs may vary in how sharply or diffusely they are represented, and such differences can shape behavior even when average expectations remain constant. Laboratory tasks that omit this learning component may not generalize well to natural decision-making contexts. Understanding how people accumulate and recall information about uncertain outcomes offers insight into the memory processes that shape belief formation and guide future decisions. We position our task within the broader framework of decisions from experience, in which individuals learn about probabilistic outcomes through sampling rather than explicit description (Hertwig & Erev, 2009). Research on the description-experience gap has demonstrated that choices based on sampled outcomes often differ systematically from choices based on explicitly described probabilities, highlighting the importance of understanding how learned experiences shape subjective representations of uncertainty (Hertwig & Erev, 2009). Our paradigm incorporates elements of both description and experience, as participants initially learn distributions with explicit probabilities and subsequently make decisions under ambiguity, where only partial information is available.

Extensive research has linked ambiguity-related behavior to adolescent risk taking (Tymula et al., 2012), autism spectrum traits (Fujino et al., 2017), vulnerability to substance use (Konova et al., 2020), physiological stress responses (FeldmanHall et al., 2016), and neural activity patterns (Blankenstein et al., 2019; Tanaka et al., 2015). However, most of this work has relied on MMEU (Gilboa & Schmeidler, 1989) as the computational framework for quantifying individual differences. These findings suggest that ambiguity aversion may be a fundamental dimension of individual differences, yet reliance on MMEU may have confounded preferences with beliefs. For example, higher ambiguity aversion in one group could reflect stronger aversion for variable risks, but it could also stem from broader or less confident beliefs about the risks. Without a way to tease these apart, existing findings remain open to reinterpretation. Overall, the reliance on MMEU leaves unclear whether such associations reflect how people value ambiguous propositions or how they form beliefs about unknown probabilities.

To address this gap, we developed the Linked Colored Lottery Task. Unlike prior studies that present probabilities explicitly or assume belief formation without directly observing it, our task embeds belief learning into the design itself. Participants first complete a learning phase where they experience different colored lotteries associated with distinct probability distributions (narrow, wide, or skewed). They then make choices between risky and ambiguous options where only the lottery color, and thus the learned distribution characteristics, is visible. This design allows us to manipulate beliefs about probability distributions while measuring preferences separately, providing the first direct test of whether MMEUbased findings reflect preferences or beliefs in an ecologically valid context.

We apply this framework to a well-replicated phenomenon, age-related differences in ambiguity aversion, that has typically been interpreted through the lens of preference-based models (Tymula et al., 2012; Blankenstein et al., 2019; Liebherr et al., 2017). If age effects reflect true preference differences, they should persist when beliefs are modeled explicitly. If they instead reflect differences in belief formation, age should correlate with belief parameters rather than preference parameters. Although we focus here on age, the implications are broader and the same tests could be put to other reported correlations or failed correlations between ambiguity preferences and individual differences.

2 Methods

2.1 Participants and Design

We conducted two experiments to test the separation of beliefs from preferences in ambiguous decision making. Experiment 1 provided an initial test of our theoretical framework in a controlled laboratory setting, while Experiment 2 replicated and extended these findings using a larger, more demographically diverse online sample. Both experiments employed the same core design: participants completed our novel Linked Colored Lottery Task, followed by questionnaires assessing individual differences. To ensure incentive compatibility, participants were informed that one randomly selected choice would determine a performance-based bonus payment.

Experiment 1 recruited 53 participants (12 female; M age = 20.9 years, SD = 1.8) from Temple University. Data collection occurred in-person as part of a larger neuroimaging study (Smith et al., 2024).

Experiment 1 was conducted in a mock fMRI environment as part of a screening session for a subsequent neuroimaging study. This context may have influenced participant arousal or attentional engagement relative to typical laboratory settings. All participants provided written informed consent under a protocol approved by Temple University's Institutional Review Board. Experiment 2 recruited 298 participants (154 female; M age = 45.4 years, SD = 15.6) via Prolific. Participants were pre-screened to match 2022 U.S. Census distributions for age, sex, and ethnicity, providing a representative sample for examining age-related differences in ambiguity preferences. The online format enabled recruitment of a larger, more diverse sample. Sample sizes were determined based on a combination of practical constraints and a priori power analysis. Experiment 1 data were collected as part of a larger neuroimaging study (Smith et al., 2024), which determined the available sample size. For Experiment 2, power analyses using α = .05 and power = .80 indicated minimum sample sizes of N = 97 for within-subject effects and N = 187 for between-subject effects, based on conservative effect size estimates (d = 0.40 within-subject; d = 0.29 between-subject). To account for potential data quality loss in online data collection, we increased the target sample size to N = 300. A sensitivity power analysis based on our final Experiment 2 analytic sample indicated 80% power (α = .05, two-tailed) to detect participant-level correlations of r ≥ .17.

Participants provided informed consent under the same IRB-approved protocol. All materials, analysis code, and data from both experiments are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/jbdenniso/LimitInfo) with detailed documentation provided in a companion data paper (Wyngaarden et al., 2025; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15122334).

2.2 Linked Colored Lottery Task

Our novel paradigm consists of two interconnected phases designed to separate beliefs from preferences in ambiguous choice. Phase 1 (Risky Colored Lottery Task) allows participants to implicitly learn probability distributions associated with different lottery colors. Phase 2 (Hidden Colored Lottery Task) measures ambiguity preferences using these learned associations, enabling us to manipulate beliefs about probability distributions while maintaining ambiguity about specific propositions.

2.2.1 Risky Colored Lottery Task

Participants made binary choices between colored lotteries, offering monetary prizes and guaranteed safe amounts. Each lottery was presented as a color-coded pie chart with a surrounding colored ring, where the bright segment indicated the probability of winning the displayed prize and the dark segment represented the probability of winning nothing (Figure 1). The exact winning probability appeared below each lottery. Outcome magnitudes were held constant across trials. In Experiment 1, lottery prizes were $13 and the safe option was $5. In Experiment 2, lottery prizes were $7 and the safe option was $3.

Lottery magnitudes were identical for risky and ambiguous options within each experiment.

Critical to our design, each color was systematically associated with a distinct probability distribution.

Participants completed 20 choices for each of three colors (red, blue, green) with colors randomly assigned to three distribution types: • Narrow distribution: Probabilities clustered around 50%, with fewer extreme values.

• Wide distribution: Probabilities clustered near extremes (0% or 100%), with fewer intermediate values.

• Skewed distribution: Probabilities clustered around 70%, with lower frequency at other values.

Color presentation order was randomized across participants. This design allowed participants to implicitly learn that each color predicted different probability characteristics, knowledge they could then apply when making ambiguous choices. Trials were time-limited in both experiments. In Experiment 1, participants had 4.5 seconds to make a choice. After the participant made a response, the remaining time was added to the intertrial interval with a minimum of 0.8 seconds. In Experiment 2, each trial lasted 4.5 seconds with an intertrial interval of 0.5 seconds. Participants could respond at any point during the trial.

Following a response, the chosen option was highlighted, the screen then went blank, and a fixation cross appeared at screen center.

2.2.2 Hidden Colored Lottery Task

Participants chose between risky lotteries (known probabilities) and "hidden" lotteries where probability information was partially or completely obscured. Crucially, the lottery color remained visible, allowing participants to use their learned associations to infer likely probability characteristics (Figure 2). Hidden lotteries displayed probability ranges (e.g., "25% to 75%") rather than exact values, creating genuine ambiguity about specific risks while providing information about possible ranges.

Experiment 1 used a fixed design where participants made seven choices for each combination of color and ambiguity level, with known probabilities ranging from 20% to 80% in 10% increments. Experiment 2 implemented an adaptive staircase procedure to more efficiently estimate individual choice patterns.

Each trial began with a 50% probability for the known lottery. Probability decreased by 10% following (Levy et al., 2012) the probability of winning is obscured either completely (a.) or partially (b.). However, the color of the ring around the lottery and portions of the lottery that are un-obscured indicate which distribution the lottery is from (e.g., narrow, wide, or skewed; e.g., Figure 1B).

2.3 Questionnaires

Following the lottery tasks, participants completed questionnaires assessing individual differences and memory for the learned probability distributions. Both experiments included the Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) and a custom memory questionnaire. The memory questionnaire assessed how well participants learned the probability distributions associated with each lottery color. For each color, participants estimated how frequently they had encountered lotteries with winning probabilities from 0% to 100% in 10% increments (i.e., 0%, 10%, 20%, etc.). These self-reported frequency estimates were crucial for fitting the SREU model, as they captured participants' beliefs about the probability distributions rather than the objective frequencies they experienced.

The memory questionnaire served a dual purpose: first, as a manipulation check to verify that participants accurately learned the color-distribution associations; and second, as input for the SREU model, which requires participants' beliefs about probability distributions rather than objective frequencies. 2.4 Data Analysis

2.4.1 Outliers and Exclusions

To ensure data quality and meaningful task engagement in online studies (Brühlmann et al., 2020), we applied two a priori exclusion criteria. First, we excluded participants who showed zero variance in memory questionnaire responses. For example, participants who reported encountering only 100% winning probabilities for all distributions clearly did not attend to the probability information, as all participants experienced the full 0-100% range.

This criterion led to the exclusion of 4 participants in Experiment 1 and 13 participants in Experiment 2. Second, we excluded participants whose risky choices violated basic economic rationality. Specifically, we excluded participants who consistently chose smaller guaranteed amounts over larger guaranteed amounts, or who chose 0% probability lotteries over guaranteed positive amounts. Under this criterion, 7 participants in Experiment 1 and 13 participants in Experiment 2 were excluded.

2.4.2 Axiom Testing

As a first step, we conducted simple theory tests to assess whether participants' choices were sensitive to learned probability distributions beyond simple range effects, a prerequisite for supporting SREU over MMEU. We first verified that participants accurately learned the distribution characteristics using their memory questionnaire responses. If participants successfully acquired the intended associations, they should report higher variance for the wide distribution compared to narrow and skewed distributions, and higher mean probability for the skewed distribution compared to wide and narrow distributions. We then tested whether learned distributions influenced choice behavior using a logistic regression. The dependent variable was participants' binary choice between risky and ambiguous lotteries during the Hidden Colored Lottery Task. Independent variables included the risky lottery's winning probability and the distribution type associated with the ambiguous lottery's color (narrow, wide, or skewed).

A significant main effect of distribution type, or an interaction between distribution and risky probability, would indicate that participants' learned beliefs influenced their decisions beyond the stated probability ranges alone. Such effects would contradict MMEU's predictions (which depend only on ranges) while supporting SREU's framework (which incorporates subjective beliefs about probability distributions).

This analysis provides a model-free test of the core theoretical distinction before proceeding to formal model comparison.

2.4.3 Computational Modeling

We fit three hierarchical Bayesian models to directly compare how well different theoretical frameworks explained participants' choices: (1) maxmin expected utility (MMEU), (2) recursive expected utility with objective beliefs (OREU), and (3) recursive expected utility with subjective beliefs (SREU).

All models used identical choice functions but differed in how they computed subjective values for ambiguous lotteries. Choices were modeled using the logistic function: where τ represents the participant-specific inverse temperature parameter capturing choice consistency.

MMEU Model: Following Levy et al. (2012), subjective value depends only on probability ranges: where A is the probability range, v is the prize value, α captures risk attitude (estimated from risky choices), and β reflects ambiguity aversion.

Positive β values indicate ambiguity aversion; negative values indicate ambiguity seeking.

REU Models: Both REU variants computed subjective value as:

We modeled preferences using a power utility function, in which the curvature parameter (φ) governs ambiguity sensitivity. Formally, v is the prize value, φ is the utility curvature parameter, and Pr(π) is the objective probability of each discrete outcome. As ϕ models preferences using a power utility function, φ values less than 1 indicate concave utility inducing ambiguity aversion, values greater than one indicate convex utility inducing ambiguity seeking, and values at exactly one indicate a linear utility inducing ambiguity neutral behavior. Though, theoretically Pr(π) may be represented continuously by each participant, we restricted this to the set of previously experienced discrete probabilities (0% to 100%, in 10% increments). The models differed in how beliefs were specified: in the objective model, μ(π) reflected the true frequencies with which a given color lottery had appeared with each probability during the task; in the subjective model, μ(π) was derived from each participant's memory reports, weighted by the frequency with which they recalled each probability for a given color.

For partially hidden lotteries, probabilities outside the known range were set to zero. The subjective model therefore incorporates each participant's own, potentially imperfect, representation of the learned distribution, whereas the objective model uses the true frequencies experienced during the task rather than participant-specific memory reports.

Model estimation used Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling implemented in PyMC (Abril-Pla et al., 2023). We employed hierarchical priors allowing individual parameters to vary around group-level means, improving estimation stability while capturing individual differences. Model comparison used leave-one-out cross-validation to compute expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD), providing robust measures of out-of-sample predictive accuracy (Vehtari et al., 2017).

This approach directly tests our central hypothesis: if MMEU adequately captures ambiguity preferences, it should outperform REU models. If beliefs matter beyond ranges, REU models should show superior fit, with SREU potentially outperforming OREU if participants' remembered experiences better predict their choices than objective frequencies.

3 Results

3.1 Memory Verification

We first tested whether participants accurately remembered the probability distributions associated with each lottery color. Across both experiments, participants reliably distinguished between distribution types based on their experiences during the risky decision task. Participants correctly reported the wide distribution as having greater variance in probabilities compared to the narrow and skewed distributions (Experiment 1 wide vs. narrow: t(45) = 7.7, p < 0.001; Experiment 1 wide vs. skew: t(45) = 7.4, p < 0.001; Experiment 2 wide vs. narrow: t(279) = 15.5, p < 0.001; Experiment 2 wide vs. skew: t(279) = 15.7, p < 0.001; Figure 3).

Participants also accurately reported the skewed distribution as having a higher mean probability of winning compared to both the narrow and wide distributions (Experiment 1 skew vs. narrow: t(45) = 12.4, p < 0.001; Experiment 1 skew vs. wide: t(45) = 7.6, p < 0.001; Experiment 2 skew vs. narrow: t(279) = 12.7, p < 0.001; Experiment 2 skew vs. wide: t(279) = 9.4, p < 0.001). These results confirm that participants successfully learned the color-distribution associations, providing the foundation for testing belief-based models of ambiguous choice.

3.2 Distribution Effects on Choice Behavior

Having established that participants learned the intended associations, we tested whether these learned beliefs influenced choice behavior beyond simple probability ranges-a critical prediction distinguishing SREU from MMEU models. We used hierarchical logistic regression to analyze choices during the hidden colored lottery task, with participants' binary choices between risky and ambiguous lotteries as the dependent variable. Independent variables included the winning probability of the risky lottery and the distribution type associated with the ambiguous lottery's color. The model included participant-level random intercepts and random slopes for all main effects, allowing for individual differences in both baseline choice tendencies and sensitivity to distribution type and risky probability. Interaction terms were modeled as fixed effects only. See table 1 for a description of average choices across distribution and level of ambiguity. Descriptive analyses indicated that the effect of learned distribution on choice behavior was consistent across both full and partial ambiguity conditions. Participants exhibited similar patterns of preference shifts across distributions under both ambiguity levels, and preliminary analyses revealed no significant interaction between ambiguity level and learned distribution. Given this null interaction, primary analyses collapse across ambiguity level to present the cleaner main effect of distribution.

Across both experiments, ambiguous lotteries associated with the skewed distribution were evaluated more favorably than those associated with the narrow or wide distributions (Figure 4). Participants were significantly more likely to choose the ambiguous option when it was linked to the skewed distribution compared to the other distributions (p < 0.001 in both experiments). For interpretability, we additionally report differences in choice probabilities between distribution conditions (see Table 1). These descriptive analyses mirror the odds-based results: participants chose the risky option more often when the ambiguous lottery was associated with the wide distribution in Experiment 1, and less often in Experiment 2, with the skewed distribution consistently producing the greatest preference for the ambiguous option across both experiments. These analyses were exploratory and not preregistered.

Although this skewed-distribution effect was statistically significant in both experiments, its absolute magnitude differed substantially. In Experiment 1, the difference in mean risky-choice percentage between the skewed distribution and the narrow and wide distributions was approximately 24 percentage points. In Experiment 2, the skewed distribution's mean risky-choice percentage was approximately 0.4 percentage points lower than that of the narrow distribution and approximately 1.9 percentage points higher than that of the wide distribution (see Table 1). The significant effect detected in Experiment 2 therefore reflects a small but statistically reliable effect, rather than an effect of comparable magnitude to that observed in Experiment 1. Note that the skewed distribution also had a higher mean probability of winning (70%) than the narrow and wide distributions (both 50%), so the conditions differed in mean winning probability as well as in distributional shape.

Importantly, Experiment 2 used an adaptive staircase procedure that adjusted the offered risky probability based on participants' preceding choices to estimate individual indifference points. Therefore, raw choice percentages should be interpreted in the context of this adaptive procedure. The logistic regression accounts for the risky probability actually offered on each trial, allowing distribution-related differences in choice to be evaluated while controlling for the offered probability. The same applies to the wide-versus-narrow comparison in Experiment 2: the 43% lower odds of a risky choice reported below is a regression estimate conditional on the offered risky probability, whereas the corresponding difference in Table 1 is approximately 2.3 percentage points (approximately 44.8% vs. 42.4%).

The first major hypothesis was that participants would exhibit aversion to variance in probability distributions. Specifically, we predicted that participants would equate ambiguous lotteries associated with the wide distribution to risky lotteries with lower chances of winning, demonstrating aversion to the higher variance. In Experiment 1, this prediction was supported: the odds of choosing the risky option were 22% higher (95% CI: [11%, 40%], p = 0.004) when the alternative ambiguous lottery was associated with the wide distribution, suggesting participants avoided the ambiguous option when it had higher variance (Figure 4).

However, Experiment 2 showed the opposite pattern. The odds of choosing the risky option were 43% lower (95% CI: [ 46%, 41%], p < 0.001) when the ambiguous lottery was associated -with the wide distribution compared to the narrow one. Importantly, Experiment 2 used an adaptive staircase procedure that adjusted the offered risky probability based on participants' preceding choices to estimate individual indifference points. Therefore, raw choice percentages should be interpreted in the context of this adaptive procedure. The logistic regression accounts for the risky probability actually offered on each trial, allowing distribution-related differences in choice to be evaluated while controlling for the offered probability. This suggests that participants' experience with the variance influenced their choices in a way that contradicts MMEU predictions and supports SREU, though the direction differed across experiments. This difference may relate to sample characteristics or contextual differences between experiments, such as the online versus in-person format or the broader age range in Experiment 2. Determining the source of this discrepancy will require future investigation.

Importantly, distribution type significantly influenced choice behavior across both experiments, indicating that participants' choices were sensitive to learned distributional information beyond probability ranges alone. This pattern is inconsistent with the core assumption of MMEU models that only probability ranges determine behavior under ambiguity.

3.3 Model Comparisons

To directly evaluate competing theoretical frameworks, we fit three hierarchical Bayesian models: maxmin expected utility (MMEU), recursive expected utility with objective beliefs (OREU), and recursive expected utility with subjective beliefs (SREU).

The SREU model contains individual information about participants' beliefs about the probabilities using their report from the memory questionnaire to help assess whether individual differences in memories can influence choice behavior. Model performance was assessed using expected log pointwise predictive density (ELPD) with leave-one-out cross-validation to compute variance around this metric (Vehtari et al., 2017). In both experiments, the subjective expected utility model showed the best fit (Experiment 1: ELPD = 156.1; Experiment 2: ELPD = 16 908.5), followed by the objective expected -utility model (Experiment 1: ΔELPD = 4.87 ± 1.87, p < 0.001; Experiment 2: ΔELPD = 384.1 ± 45.9, p < 0.001). The MMEU model performed the worst (Experiment 1: ΔELPD = 39.25 -± 7.44, p < 0.001; Experiment 2: ΔELPD = 1 565.39 ± 60.3, p < 0.001; Figure 5). These results indicate that recursive expected utility frameworks consistently outperform MMEU models. As the SREU model outperforms the "objective" REU model as well, we can say that incorporating participants' subjective beliefs about probability distributions further improves predictive accuracy beyond using objective frequencies alone. Posterior predictive checks comparing observed and model-predicted proportions of risky choices in Experiment 2 for the MMEU and SREU models are reported in the Supplementary Materials (Supplementary Figure S1 and Supplementary Table S1).

3.4 Individual Differences: Age and Belief Formation

Our final test examined whether age-related differences in ambiguity aversion reflect preference differences or belief differences. We analyzed data from Experiment 2, which provided sufficient age variation for this analysis (Experiment 1's narrow age range precluded meaningful age-related analyses). Age showed systematic correlations with participants' reported belief distributions. We additionally examined whether age was associated with the central tendency of subjective belief distributions. Age was not significantly correlated with the implied mean of the skewed distribution (r = 0.099, p -correlation with the implied mean of the narrow distribution (r = 0.141, p = 0.028). This pattern suggests that age-related differences are more consistently expressed in the dispersion of subjective beliefs rather than their central tendency. Age was positively correlated with the standard deviation of the narrow distribution (r = 0.21, p = 0.001), negatively correlated with the wide distribution (r = -0.30, p < 0.001), and positively correlated with the skewed distribution (r = 0.29, p < 0.001; Figure 6).

Crucially, when we examined the relationship between age and the φ parameter from the SREU model, which captures individual ambiguity aversion based on beliefs about ambiguous probabilities, we found no significant relationship (r = 0.03, p = 0.45). The φ parameter captures individual differences in sensitivity to ambiguity, with values below 1 indicating ambiguity aversion, values above 1 indicating ambiguity seeking, and a value of exactly 1 indicating ambiguity neutrality. For robustness, as many studies find their samples are largely ambiguity averse; we specifically examine this relationship for participants displaying ambiguity aversion (N = 196) and find that results remain null (r = -0.03, p = 0.54).

These findings suggest that some previously reported age differences in ambiguity-related choice may reflect age-related differences in how probabilistic information is represented or learned, rather than differences in ambiguity preferences alone. However, the present data do not allow us to identify the specific cognitive mechanisms responsible for these associations, and this interpretation should be treated cautiously. Separating beliefs from preferences nonetheless provides a useful analytical distinction, as age appears more consistently associated with belief-related measures than with the preference parameter in our models. participants' age and the ambiguity aversion parameter reflecting preferences in the REU model. Shaded regions represent 95% confidence intervals around regression estimates. 4 Discussion Overall, we find that individual beliefs about the probabilities can influence ambiguous decisions and represent a meaningful individual difference that can be represented at the computational level for decisions. Across two experiments, the subjective recursive expected utility (SREU) model consistently outperformed the widely used maxmin expected utility (MMEU) model, indicating that people's choices depend not only on probability ranges but on their beliefs about probability distributions. The subjective model incorporates each participant's own, potentially imperfect, representation of the learned These findings challenge the theoretical foundations of a substantial body of research on individual differences in ambiguity aversion. Studies linking ambiguity preferences to autism spectrum traits (Fujino et al., 2017), substance use vulnerability (Konova et al., 2020), stress responses (FeldmanHall et al., 2016), and developmental differences (Tymula et al., 2012) have relied almost exclusively on MMEU-based interpretations. Our results suggest that many of these associations may reflect differences in belief formation rather than stable preference traits. Prior work has shown that belief formation under uncertainty can be systematically asymmetric, although the direction of this asymmetry is not fully consistent across studies. Some evidence suggests that unfavorable information may exert a stronger influence on ambiguity-related choices (e.g., Peysakhovich & Karmarkar, 2016), whereas other work finds that favorable cues can disproportionately shape valuation (e.g., Krefeld-Schwalb et al., 2024).

Rather than indicating a single dominant bias, these findings suggest that asymmetric belief updating may depend on contextual factors such as task structure, information presentation, or learning dynamics.

Future work relating ambiguity to individual psychological traits should take care that beliefs and preferences are properly distinguished, what appear to be preference-based individual differences may actually represent cognitive differences in how people process and remember probabilistic information.

The implications extend beyond ambiguity research to broader questions about cognitive mechanisms underlying decision making. If belief formation varies systematically across clinical populations, age groups, or other individual difference dimensions, then studies using models that confound beliefs with preferences may fundamentally mischaracterize the psychological mechanisms underlying choice behavior. Our findings suggest that many documented individual differences attributed to preferences may instead reflect variation in learning, memory encoding, or probabilistic reasoning. These cognitive processes are amenable to different theoretical and empirical approaches than affective evaluation of uncertainty. One speculative possibility is that older adults place greater weight on prior expectations about how dispersed probabilities usually are. This could pull estimates toward a common prior, making narrow distributions look more variable and wide distributions less variable, consistent with the opposite age associations we actually observed. Age-related differences in memory or encoding precision offer an alternative, non-exclusive possibility. The present data cannot adjudicate among these accounts, and we offer them here only as candidate directions for future work.

Our methodological contribution addresses a critical gap in how researchers study ambiguity in laboratory settings. The Linked Colored Lottery Task captures key features of real-world ambiguous decision making, where people must learn about uncertainty through experience rather than explicit probability descriptions, while maintaining experimental control. This distinction between descriptionbased and experience-based learning is increasingly recognized as a fundamental dimension of risk perception, as repeated experiences can shape subjective beliefs about uncertainty in ways that differ substantially from information acquired through symbolic descriptions alone (Hertwig & Wulff, 2022).

This approach enables researchers to manipulate beliefs about probability distributions systematically, providing a more ecologically valid platform for studying ambiguity preferences. The task's ability to separate objective experiences from subjective beliefs offers a powerful tool for investigating how memory, attention, and other cognitive processes shape decision making. Several limitations warrant consideration. We observed different patterns of ambiguity aversion across experiments, with Experiment 1 participants showing traditional ambiguity aversion while Experiment 2 participants appeared ambiguity-seeking. These differences likely reflect multiple contextual factors that we did not fully control. Experiment 1 was conducted in-person in a laboratory setting with a relatively homogeneous group of young adults, whereas Experiment 2 was conducted online with a much broader age range and more diverse participant pool. This hybrid structure connects our findings to the description-experience gap literature, suggesting that experience-based learning may shape subjective probability representations in ways that influence ambiguity preferences. In particular, variability in sampling or encoding during learning may contribute to the ambiguity-seeking patterns observed in Experiment 2. Laboratory settings typically minimize distractions and provide more consistent engagement, while online environments may introduce greater variability in attention, comprehension, or motivation, potentially altering how variance information is encoded and applied during choice ( Brühlmann et al., 2020).

Payment structure differences may also contribute to these contrasting findings, as different incentive mechanisms can systematically influence risk and ambiguity preferences (Huber et al., 2023). Our findings also complement prior evidence that information processing under ambiguity is systematically biased. Specifically, when participants receive larger guaranteed payments (as in Experiment 1), additional task earnings may be perceived as "house money," whereas smaller baseline endowments (as in Experiment 2) may frame task earnings as more consequential losses or gains.

Several procedural factors differ across the two experiments -including testing setting, sample composition, payment structure, and staircase procedure -and the present design cannot isolate which of these factors, individually or in combination, is responsible for the observed reversal in the direction of the ambiguity-seeking effect. We note, however, that ambiguity seeking in Experiment 2 was observed across all three learned distributions (Table 1), suggesting a general shift in ambiguity preference rather than an effect confined to a particular learned distribution.

We also considered whether age might account for the difference in ambiguity attitudes between experiments. Within Experiment 2, we found no relationship between age and the ambiguity-preference parameter (see Individual Differences: Age and Belief Formation, above). However, because age cued probability structures. Thus, while it captures one important feature of natural decision making, its generalizability to real-world settings remains limited.

Future research should extend this framework to investigate how belief formation interacts with learning and decision making across diverse populations and contexts. Such extensions may be particularly important for connecting laboratory measures of ambiguity to real-world decision environments, where attention, memory, and learning processes interact with delayed feedback, complex choice sets, and social sources of information (Olschewski et al., 2024). Consistent with evidence that framing and task goals influence what is selectively encoded and later retrieved, our results suggest that how ambiguous information is presented during learning may alter memory-based belief formation (Murphy & Knowlton, 2022).

The SREU approach provides a foundation for understanding how individual differences in memory, attention, and probabilistic reasoning shape choices under uncertainty. Our findings further suggest that ambiguity-related choices depend on how people store and update information about uncertain experiences, linking belief formation directly to memory-based learning.

Researchers should consider incorporating belief elicitation measures into existing paradigms as a lowcost method for distinguishing preference-based from belief-based explanations of behavioral differences (Danese et al., 2017). Looking ahead, future studies may apply the SREU framework to better understand how belief-based ambiguity interacts with reward learning, as many reinforcement learning paradigms begin with ambiguity that fades with feedback (Hayden et al., 2010). Ultimately, recognizing that ambiguous decision making depends on both what people believe and how they feel about uncertainty opens new avenues for understanding the psychological mechanisms that drive behavior across individuals and contexts. More broadly, these findings highlight ambiguity as a window into fundamental cognitive processes of belief construction and evaluation, offering a framework that connects decisionmaking behavior with core theories of learning, reasoning, and cognition.

5 Conclusions

Ambiguity pervades many decisions in daily life, and understanding how people respond to it remains a central challenge in decision science. Yet a crucial piece of this picture may be missing. Prior work has often conflated what people believe with how they feel about uncertainty. By developing a novel experimental paradigm that disentangles beliefs from preferences, we show that the subjective recursive expected utility (SREU) model provides superior explanations of choice behavior compared to the widely used maxmin expected utility (MMEU) framework. Most significantly, individual differences previously attributed to ambiguity preferences, including the robust association between age and ambiguity aversion, were better accounted for by differences in belief formation than by preference parameters, suggesting that prior interpretations based solely on MMEU may need reexamination.

The observed relationship between age and increased dispersion of subjective belief for the narrow and skewed distribution but decreasing for the wide distribution may suggest that these effects are related to learning. One speculative possibility is that this pattern reflects a prior for the probabilities that becomes more entrenched with age, although the present data cannot adjudicate among alternative accounts. This provides a potential reinterpretation of prior findings linking age to ambiguity aversion, as increased uncertainty in belief representations may manifest behaviorally as greater avoidance of ambiguous options when beliefs and preferences are not explicitly dissociated.

These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how researchers interpret individual differences in economic decision making. Studies across behavioral economics, clinical psychology, and developmental research have relied heavily on MMEU-based interpretations to link ambiguity preferences to psychological traits and neurobiological differences. Our results suggest that many of these associations may need reinterpretation through the lens of belief-based rather than preference-based mechanisms. This distinction has profound implications for understanding economic behavior across populations and designing interventions that target the appropriate psychological processes.

The integration of belief-based models like SREU into the study of decision making under uncertainty represents a crucial step toward more accurate and comprehensive theories of economic behavior.

By distinguishing cognitive processes that shape beliefs from affective processes that determine uncertainty attitudes, and recognizing that these may contribute differently across individuals and contexts, researchers can develop more nuanced accounts of how individuals navigate the pervasive uncertainty that characterizes real-world decision making.

Importantly, the reversal in the direction of the variance effect corresponds to the broader difference in ambiguity attitudes across experiments. Experiment 1 participants showed ambiguity aversion, whereas Experiment 2 participants appeared ambiguity-seeking. Thus, the reversal in how participants evaluated ambiguous options associated with the wide distribution is consistent with this broader shift in ambiguity preference. Although the direction of the variance effect did not replicate, the influence of learned distributional information on ambiguity-related choice was evident in both experiments.

Although the direction of the variance effect differs between experiments, the subjective-belief model outperforms the objective-belief model in both experiments. We do not attempt to offer a single explanation for the reversal in direction, as several contextual and procedural factors differed between the experiments (see also our discussion of Experiment 2 ambiguity seeking above).

The differing patterns observed across experiments also warrant further investigation. Future work should examine how demographic characteristics, task context, and learning processes jointly influence ambiguity-related decisions. Additional methodological constraints should be acknowledged. Our manipulation of participants' experiences with the distributions may have altered the belief formation process, whereas previous studies without such explicit exposure may have captured more spontaneous belief formation (e.g., Levy et al., 2010; Fujino et al., 2017; FeldmanHall et al., 2016). Finally, although our paradigm is more naturalistic than traditional urn-based tasks because it requires learning probability distributions from experience, it remains a laboratory simplification. Lotteries were randomly presented on either the left or right side of the screen. (b) Three histograms representing how often color lotteries assigned a narrow, wide, and skewed distribution were presented with a particular chance of winning the prize (Experiment 1: $13; Experiment 2: $7).

risky choices and increased by 10% following ambiguous choices. Step sizes halved after participants switched choices twice, and increased by half after two consecutive identical choices, providing precise estimates of individual indifference points while constraining probabilities within a 0-100% range. This paradigm enables direct comparison of MMEU and SREU models: if choices depend only on probability ranges (supporting MMEU), lottery colors should have no effect beyond their associated ranges. If choices depend on learned probability distributions (supporting SREU), different colors should produce systematically different choice patterns even when ranges are identical.
